do_not_say.avoid: The twenty-mile rule bars these licences.
do_not_say.why: The rule was repealed effective 1 January 2026 by P.A. 25-101 sections 15 to 17. It supports no current compliance finding of any kind.
do_not_say.say: Former CGS 21a-420u(f), repealed effective 1 January 2026, applied between 1 July 2023 and 31 December 2025. As a historical question the record shows [x].

do_not_say.why: No public Connecticut record establishes legal or beneficial ownership of any cannabis establishment. Across 4,702 typed relationships there is not one ownership edge.
do_not_say.say: Company A is filed as a principal of Company B in the Secretary of the State registry. A principal filing proves the filing, not ownership, a percentage or control.

do_not_say.avoid: A contribution or an award caused a decision.
do_not_say.why: Contributions, awards and event attendance are lawful, disclosed and ordinary. Sequence is not causation and the record does not support a causal claim.
do_not_say.say: X contributed $N on [date]; the decision followed on [date]. No link between the two is established and none is asserted.

do_not_say.avoid: The social equity ventures are fronts.
do_not_say.why: Neither limb of the statutory test can be checked from outside: no ownership percentage is published and control was not defined until 1 November 2026.
do_not_say.say: Whether these ventures meet the fifty per cent ownership and control test cannot be determined from any public Connecticut record, in either direction.

do_not_say.avoid: Operator X has N per cent of the Connecticut cannabis market.
do_not_say.why: Connecticut publishes no sales or revenue by licensee. Any market share figure is unsourceable.
do_not_say.say: Operator X holds N of the M active retail credentials, which is licence concentration, not market share.

do_not_say.avoid: The lottery was won by X.
do_not_say.why: The published applicant list records entries bought, not awards made.
do_not_say.say: X appears in the published lottery applicant list with N entries. The list does not record awards.

do_not_say.avoid: A witness’s position is what the committee report says it is.
do_not_say.why: Joint favorable reports summarize testimony in committee staff’s words.
do_not_say.say: The committee report characterises the testimony as [x]; the witness’s own filing says [y].

do_not_say.avoid: The requirement is in the regulations.
do_not_say.why: Many adult-use requirements sit in an agency policy document, not in regulations adopted under chapter 54.
do_not_say.say: The requirement appears in the Department’s Policies and Procedures, which is not a regulation adopted under chapter 54.

do_not_say.avoid: The bill’s sponsor wrote this language.
do_not_say.why: Bill status records give introducers and LCO numbers, not drafting authorship.
do_not_say.say: The language first appears in [instrument] on [date]. Who requested it is unknown on this record; the earliest source found is [x].

do_not_say.avoid: This agency failed to adopt required regulations.
do_not_say.why: Whether a regulation was required, and by when, depends on the enabling section and any later amendment. State the section and the date before the conclusion.
do_not_say.say: [Section] directed the agency to adopt regulations by [date]. The eRegulations record shows [status] as of [date].

claims.claim: Connecticut cannabis law changed in 463 discrete enacted sections across the eight acts whose text is held, between 2021 and 2026.
The three twenty-mile separation rules were repealed by P.A. 25-101 sections 15 to 17, signed 24 June 2025, effective 1 January 2026, and no later act restores them.
The General Assembly’s published chapter 420h page still printed the repealed subsection in full on 29 September 2026.
683 written testimony records were filed across 14 cannabis bills in six sessions; 124 of them state a position of Supports and 339 state Opposes.
Who drafted any particular amendment is unknown for almost every amendment in this dataset.
No public Connecticut record establishes legal ownership or operational control of any cannabis establishment.
Adult-use cannabis requirements are carried by an agency Policies and Procedures document rather than by regulations adopted under chapter 54.
Four Social Equity Council rulemakings on equity joint venture ownership and control were withdrawn permanently.
Trade association awards and events preceded decisions favourable to award recipients.
Lobbying by cannabis clients caused specific statutory language.
The Chamber’s five-point list appears in a subsequent substitute bill.
Records show one laboratory printed a 1,000,000 CFU/g aerobic pass line on 2,253 product registrations from 2018 to 2022, and the investigation found no state instrument that set it.
Records show DCP's own 2026 bill struck the statutory Aspergillus and qPCR requirements, and its written testimony described that section only as a disposal deadline.
Records show no adult-use cannabis regulation has ever been codified; testing rests on policies that lapse on 1 July 2028, and from 1 October 2026 the statute points to regulations not yet adopted.
Records show three 2024 product registrations rest on certificates that record E. coli 'Detected' and print 'Pass'; sale of those batches is not established.
Records show the equity loan fund lent $2,980,000 to five borrowers, and auditors found tax-return and collateral gaps on the loans they reviewed.
Comptroller records show the Social Equity and Innovation Fund spent 2.7% of the $68.8 million it had in fiscal 2025.
Records show auditors found no approval on file for any subgrant in the $6 million reinvestment pilot; the Prosperity Foundation wire loss was already reported.
Records show the five-year exit from equity joint ventures first appears in a floor amendment offered by three House members, including the Majority Leader; the drafter is unknown.
Records show Verano lists two Council-approved equity ventures in its table of controlled entities, and one of them guarantees Verano's 2026 credit facility.

Records show a state loan, lobbying registrations, private capital and a GTI-named entity meet in the Budr group, and a former senator is listed in the ownership chain of the largest borrower; the sequence is documented, but influence is not established.
Honest A-F completion at C-383 is 31.9%.
Gate One is not complete, no records requests have been sent, PACER has not been pulled, and no one named here has been asked for comment.
Records show AltaSci Laboratories printed a yeast-and-mould criterion of less than 1,000,000 CFU/g on 404 raw-flower and pre-roll product registrations.
Those 404 registrations rest on 197 distinct certificate files.
The criterion appears in two windows: 31 August to 9 December 2020 (149 registrations, 83 files) and 20 July 2021 to 21 January 2022 (255 registrations, 114 files).
Between the windows, the lab's certificates printed 10,000.
Records show a separate aerobic-count criterion of less than 1,000,000 CFU/g on 2,253 registrations, backed by 1,207 certificate files, from February 2018 to January 2022.
The move from 10,000 to 1,000,000 is 100-fold.
The 1,000,000 ceiling is 10 times the 100,000 limit the state adopted in 2022.
All 83 window-A certificates print no Aspergillus test.
All 114 window-B certificates print an Aspergillus test.
According to CT Insider (Ginny Monk, 6 December 2021), DCP approved AltaSci's yeast-and-mould request by email in August 2020, and the reported approval paired the change with Aspergillus testing.
The investigation found no formal regulatory instrument authorising either criterion in the regulations and policies it read.
In 5,233 parsed AltaSci certificates the project found no failed plating-count test; 543 certificates lack a parsed microbial result.
Records show AltaSci's state laboratory credentials lapsed in early 2024.
Records show a Secretary of the State notice of intent to dissolve AltaSci LLC, filed on 11 August 2026.
According to CT Insider (December 2021), DCP approved AltaSci's yeast-and-mould change by email in August 2020; that report is the prior coverage.
According to the ledger, Connecticut Public (Kate Seltzer, 22 March 2023) also covered the change and dated the approval to 2021; the certificates contradict that date.
The project adds a full certificate census: two separate windows, the missing Aspergillus test in window A, and a four-year aerobic criterion for which no coverage was located.
It is not established that DCP approved the aerobic criterion or the 2021 window.
No harm to any patient is established; a printed criterion is not a measured result.
The project does not hold the August 2020 approval emails.
DCP may have sanctioned both windows by email, and indoor medical flower can test clean, which would also explain the universal pass rate.
Records show SB 231 (2026) was raised by the General Law Committee 'on behalf of the Department of Consumer Protection'.
Records show its Section 1 struck the statutory analyte list, the Aspergillus mandate and the certified qPCR method from CGS 21a-408w.
Records show HB 5350 carried the same deletion when it was introduced.
The deletion is not among the 24 substantive changes listed in HB 5350's Statement of Purpose.
DCP's written testimony on SB 231 (23 February 2026) explains Sections 1 and 4 only as setting 'a timeframe for the destruction of cannabis that has failed testing'.
That testimony does not mention the deletion.

The committee report records an opponent objecting that the bill 'removes statutory testing requirements and replaces them with agency-controlled policies'; that opponent is the journalist who runs this project.
Records show the deletion became law through HB 5350, as P.A. 26-8 section 44.
None of the seven floor transcripts contains the words Aspergillus, polymerase or qPCR.
The one direct floor question about section 44 was answered with the remediation process only.
None of the 22 floor amendments addressed the deletion.
The OLR bill analysis dated 21 April 2026, before the Senate votes, described the move of testing standards from statute to DCP regulations, without naming Aspergillus or qPCR.
DCP policy PR2024-040 still requires Aspergillus and qPCR testing until 1 July 2028.

Records show a five-point testing list from CT Cannabis Chamber of Commerce testimony (19 March 2025) appeared word for word in sHB 7178 section 21 five days later; that text was later removed from the bill.
According to the story card, the only prior coverage of the deletion is an opinion column by Lou Rinaldi (CT Examiner, 22 May 2026; republished CT Mirror, 4 June 2026).
The project adds that DCP proposed the deletion in its own bill, that its testimony described a different purpose, and that the floor record and all 22 amendments did not name it.
Why DCP proposed the deletion is not established.
No record shows who asked for it; the earlier reading that industry asks drove it (L-0198) is disproven.
Moving technical analyte lists from statute to rule matches practice in other states, and the requirement still stands in policy until 2028.
Queries of every cannabis section series of the state regulations return no adult-use cannabis regulation.
Records show medical cannabis testing has a codified regulation, RCSA 21a-408-60, effective 13 June 2022.
Records show DCP withdrew its adult-use codification package, PR2024-053, on 11 June 2025, and the docket states no reason.
Records show the Legislative Regulation Review Committee rejected two DCP cannabis regulations in May 2025.
Records show adult-use rules rest on DCP operational policies that CGS 21a-421j(b) gives 'the force and effect of law'.
Thirteen adult-use testing requirements in those policies lose force on 1 July 2028.
As of 21 September 2026, no testing regulation is pending; the only new adult-use records are Council policies on eligibility and ownership (PR2026-040 and PR2026-045).

Before P.A. 26-8, the statute required only posting and filing with the Secretary of the State; the duty to submit these policies to the legislative committee was added by P.A. 26-8 (sections 31, 58, 73, 78 and 79).

Across 1,122 statute chapters, the explicit formula of force-of-law policies issued notwithstanding sections 4-168 to 4-172 appears in 12 sections, and 11 of them concern cannabis, hemp or cannabis tax.
Other agencies can act before rulemaking by other routes, such as Revenue Services 'rulings in lieu of regulations'.
According to the ledger, prior coverage reported only the May 2025 LRRC rejections (Citizen Portal, an AI meeting summary; CT News Junkie headline, 28 May 2025).
The project adds the full census, the unexplained withdrawal, the 2028 expiry of 13 testing requirements and the late committee-submission duty.
DCP's reason for withdrawing PR2024-053 is not established.
Whether DCP filed a written explanation under CGS 4-170b or 4-171 is not established.
The legislature built the policy route on purpose as a transition device in 2021, and LRRC rejections are part of normal review.

Records show that from 1 October 2026, CGS 21a-408w(a)(1) (P.A. 26-8 section 44) and new section 52 require testing under 'the laboratory testing standards established in the regulations adopted ... pursuant to section 21a-421j'.
As of 21 September 2026, no regulation under 21a-421j, emergency or permanent, had been adopted.
Records show the only codified testing rule, RCSA 21a-408-60, was adopted under a different section, 21a-408r.
Neither P.A. 26-100 nor any 2026 special session changed that wording.
The same act uses broader wording elsewhere, naming 'regulations, policies and procedures' in sections 64 and 94.
No coverage was located; the OLR analysis describes the standards as set 'in DCP regulations'.
This is a text reading by the project, flagged for counsel.
It is not established that testing requirements lapse; that is a legal question.
DCP can argue that its force-of-law policies, which must set laboratory testing standards, satisfy the reference until 1 July 2028.
Records show DCP approved three product registrations on 12 to 14 November 2024: Theraplant MMBR.0024873, CTPharma MMBR.0024806 and Curaleaf MMBR.0024890.
Records show each registration rests on a Northeast Laboratories certificate from tests run 29 October to 1 November 2024.
Records show each certificate records enteropathogenic E. coli as 'Detected' against a 'Not Detected' limit and prints 'Pass' for microbiology.
The 'Not Detected' limit was the limit in force under policy PR2024-029.
In the project's re-test of 33,581 certificates, these are 3 of 5 in-force failures; the other 2 were correctly marked as failures.
The investigation found no recall, alert or enforcement action for these products in the searched materials.
Among 77 DCP notices to cannabis establishments from June 2023 to September 2026, the investigation found no recall, product hold or advisory.
A licensee duty to report recalls to DCP took effect on 12 November 2024.

According to the ledger, the three certificates were first flagged in a privately held analysis supplied to the project (Report #87); distribution beyond counsel is not verified, and no press coverage was located.
The project adds the census denominator, the limit in force on the test date, the approval dates and the negative recall search.
It is not established that the tested batches were sold.
No harm is established, and DCP's awareness is not established.

The assay (AOAC 2017.01) is a screening method, so a presumptive positive may have been cleared by a confirmatory test that the certificate does not show, or the 'Pass' cell may be a lab-system reporting defect.
Records show DCP's 16 March 2022 Notice of Decision states that Medicinal Genomics (MGC) proposed replacing plating with qPCR.
Records show the same document lists MGC among the experts DCP consulted before drafting.
According to its own comment letters, MGC sells molecular test products for cannabis.
Records show adult-use policy PR2023-024 switched the required method to a molecular method on 1 July 2023, without rulemaking.
For about a year the medical and adult-use programmes required different test methods for the same plant.
On the same 2022 record, industry commenters argued against the higher 100,000 limit.
According to the story card, Ginny Monk (CT Insider, 7 February 2022) reported the proposal and comments, not the proponent-consultee overlap or the later policy switch.
The project adds the overlap between proponent and consultee, and the later method switch by policy.
It is not established that MGC's advice decided the outcome.
What DCP knew or disclosed about MGC's commercial interest is not established.
MGC is a recognised authority on cannabis microbiology, qPCR has technical advantages, and consulting vendors is common.
Records show P.A. 26-8 section 52(c)(3) deems a remediation plan for a microbially failed batch approved if DCP sends no written notice within 60 days, from 1 October 2026.
Records show the act lists ionizing radiation among permitted remediation methods for failed flower.
Connecticut certificates of analysis have never recorded whether a batch was remediated.
Records show the state's mandatory point-of-sale notice says remediation processes 'have not been thoroughly studied for potential health impacts'.
Records show the LRRC rejected PR2025-010, the mandatory rule for moderate-THC hemp-product vendors under CGS 21a-426(l), without prejudice on 27 January 2026.
Under the project's reading of CGS 4-170(e), resubmission was due by 3 March 2026.
As of 21 September 2026 the docket shows no resubmission.

According to the story cards, remediation and irradiation were covered in opinion columns (Lou Rinaldi, CT Mirror, 5 August 2025 and 4 June 2026) and trade reporting (Hartford Business Journal, 6 March 2023); no coverage of the hemp deadline was located.
The project adds the enacted 60-day default, the missing certificate field and the missed hemp deadline.
How many remediation plans DCP has received, approved or let lapse into approval is not established.
DCP's reason for not resubmitting the hemp rule is not established, and the 4-170(e) text could not be re-fetched live.
Deemed-approval clauses are a standard answer to agency backlog, DCP still reviews each plan, and DCP met both resubmission deadlines on its cannabis packages.
Records show the Canna-Business Revolving Loan Fund made seven loans totalling $2,980,000 to five borrowers.
The borrowers are Connecticut Social Equity LLC (Rodeo), Connecticut Cannabis Courier I LLC, BUDR HOLDING 6 LLC, Dutch LLC and Lorrain's CT LLC.
Records show the Council's public loan totals reconcile to state payment records.
According to Council reports, 18 applicants sought over $7 million in October 2024, and a backlog of 30 applications was reported by May 2025.
Records show the Comptroller's 2024 examination counted 19 applications seeking $8.55 million, none funded as of 1 August 2024.
The unsuccessful applicants are not public.
Records show state auditors reviewed three loan projects with $1,480,000 in spending as of May 2025.
Records show the auditors found the Council 'did not obtain all the required investor tax returns prior to approving two loan applications'.
Records show they also found it did not adequately address a collateral concern raised by the Office of Financial Review and Compliance on one application, and had no written loan-fund procedures.
By payment dates, the three reviewed loans are Dutch LLC, Rodeo and Lorrain's CT LLC; the auditors do not say which two lacked returns.
Loan decisions are DECD and Council staff actions; no Council vote on a loan is recorded.
The investigation found no state UCC lien on any borrower in the searched filings.
Records show borrowers whose affiliates were registered lobbying clients received $2.0 million of the $2.98 million lent.

According to the ledger, the Comptroller's 2024 examination and same-day coverage (NBC Connecticut, Inside Investigator, CT Mirror, 23 September 2024) reported programme delays, and the 2026 audit's headline items were reported (CT News Junkie, 30 July 2026; CT Insider, 31 July 2026).
The project adds the borrower-by-borrower portfolio, its reconciliation, the audit matched to the first three loans, the staff-only decision design, the lien search and the lobbying overlap.
No link between lobbying and any loan decision has been found.
Because unsuccessful applicants and their eligibility are not public, no concentration or selection conclusion can be drawn.
Tax returns may have been obtained after approval, the applicant pool may have held many ineligible applications, and lobbying registration is lawful.
Comptroller records show fund 12073, the Social Equity and Innovation Fund, had $68,846,143 available in fiscal 2025.
Records show it spent $1,861,961, or 2.7%, and closed the year at $66,984,182.
Records show $34,658,668 came in from account 35689, which showed no spending in fiscal 2023 or 2024.
Records show P.A. 23-204 made the equity funds depend on appropriation and barred rescission by the budget office.
Records show the same act required $5 million to move from the equity account to the General Fund at the end of fiscal 2023.
The Comptroller schedules show the $34,658,668 carried forward intact and the same amount reaching the fund in 2025, which is consistent with the $5 million never being taken from this account.
Records show the Council's 'sole discretion' over equity spending was first written in 2023, by P.A. 23-204.
Records show the Comptroller recommended in September 2024 that the legislature define how the Council may use appropriated funds (Recommendation 5).

Records show P.A. 25-168 then made 'sole discretion' the permanent rule for a new account from 1 July 2025 and repealed the fund whose money could be spent only through appropriation for listed purposes.
Records show the Council told auditors in 2026 that it disagrees with the recommendation to define its uses in statute.

According to the story card, earlier reports said the Council held about $34 million undistributed in 2023 and 2024 (Inside Investigator, 3 October 2023 and 23 September 2024; Mark Pazniokas, CT Mirror, 23 June 2024).
According to the ledger, Connecticut Public reported the Comptroller's recommendation on 24 September 2024.
The project adds the fiscal 2025 totals, the source account with two years of nil spending, the untaken transfer, and the later statutory choice not to follow the recommendation.
Encumbrances and commitments at 30 June 2025 are not established.
The transfer journals have not been seen, so a transfer booked elsewhere is not excluded.
Budgetary cash figures exclude encumbrances and loan spending booked to other accounts, and the $36 million grant round was awarded in December 2025, after the year closed.
Records show the Council paid The Prosperity Foundation (TPF) $1,000,000 on 8 June 2023 under contract 23SECCOMREIPILOT004.
Records show the Council paid Hispanic Federation $1,000,000 in June 2023 under contract 23SECCOMREIPILOT006.
Records show auditors found the Council had no documentation approving any subrecipient award under any of the six pilot managers (Finding 20).
Records show $45,704 of unspent subgrant funds was later recovered.

Records show Finding 19, headed 'Social Equity Council Misappropriation of State Funds', concerns one grant recipient that could not return $20,684, and faults the Council for not alerting DECD or freezing funds.
Records show Finding 22 says staff negotiated two sole-source support contracts without budget-office preapproval, which the auditors called 'a clear violation' of procurement standards.
Records show the Council agreed with Findings 19 to 22.
Records show the Comptroller's 2024 review of the selection of all six grant managers found 'We did not identify any exceptions'.
TPF's amended 2023 tax return states that $900,000 was stolen by wire fraud on 21 August 2023 and $399,155 was recovered, a loss of $500,845.
The theft came 74 days after the Council payment.

Records show TPF's 2023 single audit named the Council grant as its major programme, reported nothing passed to subrecipients, and recorded a material weakness for being 'unable to produce records supporting the work performed'.
According to the New Haven Independent (21 November 2023), TPF distributed $900,000 to 25 organisations with Council seed money.
Records show Hispanic Federation's 11 December 2023 release named Blue Hills Civic Association (BHCA) among its pilot grantees of 'up to $100,000'.
Records show the DECD-commissioned forensic audit lists 'Hispanic Federation $100,000.00' in BHCA's fiscal 2024 grant revenue.
That this $100,000 was Council pilot money is a strong inference.

Records show a separate $1,100,000 of a DECD legislative grant passed from BHCA to TPF in December 2023, and the forensic audit found $771,876 of it unspent and not observed returned; that money was General Fund money, not cannabis revenue.
Records show that since 6 June 2024, CGS 21a-420d(n) requires the Council to approve subgrant amounts, grantees and purposes.
For the next round, records show a Council committee voted region-by-region rosters of 173 subgrantees in August 2026, and final Council votes were scheduled for 8 September 2026.

According to the story card, the wire loss, BHCA's unsupported spending and the audit headline were already reported (Edmund H. Mahony, Hartford Courant, 31 July 2025; Marc E. Fitch, Inside Investigator, 26 January 2026; Andrew Brown, CT Mirror, 2 September 2026; Viktoria Sundqvist, CT News Junkie, 30 July 2026).
The project ties those reports back to one programme: the missing subgrant approvals, the payment date and 74-day interval, the single-audit line, and the Hispanic Federation route to BHCA.
It is not established that Council money was in the stolen transfer.
It is not established which 'funder' told TPF it did not expect repayment.
TPF held other money besides the Council grant, grant payments often cross fiscal years, and Hispanic Federation may have paid BHCA from other funds.

According to automatic captions of the Council's own video of its 4 March 2025 meeting, Councilor Avery Gaddis described calls from roughly half a dozen to a dozen elected officials seeking to change loan decisions.
Records show the approved minutes of that meeting compress the discussion to one sentence.
The audio has not been verified, because YouTube was blocked and no CT-N copy was found; the caption text is a provisional paraphrase, not a quotation.
No prior coverage was located.
The project adds the video account and documents its gap with the approved minutes.
No official, applicant or changed decision is named.
No effect of the calls on any loan is established.
Calls from officials may be lawful constituent casework, and the Council says it resisted.
Records show that on 2 December 2025 the Council approved the ten-region grant-manager slate on a motion by Gaddis, seconded by Naeem, with only Jefferson abstaining.
Records show seven members who voted for that slate declared regional conflicts on 26 August 2026 and recused from those regions' subgrantee rosters.
The 2026 declarations concerned subgrantee rosters, not the grant managers themselves.
Records show the $29.95 million fiscal 2027 budget passed on 1 September 2026 with one recusal (Hawkins).
Records show that in 2023 Councilor Gaddis, an officer of a $10,000 pilot subgrantee, abstained on that grantee's award.
Records show an 'Edwin Shirley' as co-principal with TPF chair Howard K. Hill of two LLCs, one registered on 8 August 2023, 61 days after the Council paid TPF.
That this is Councilor Edwin Shirley is a strong inference, not a confirmed identity.
Shirley was absent from the 2023 TPF vote.
Records show the Comptroller recommended in 2024 that the Council adopt an ethics code.
A negative screen found no Council member on the boards of the round-two managers, TPF or Hispanic Federation.

According to the story card, only the Comptroller's ethics-code recommendation was reported (NBC Connecticut, Inside Investigator, CT Mirror, 23 September 2024); no coverage of these joins was located.
The project tests that recommendation against actual votes and registry ties.
No conflict under ethics rules is established.
No outcome disparity is shown: tied organisations did not receive more.
Regional conflicts may arise only at the subgrantee stage, which is when members recused.
Records show Budr and Fine Fettle representatives asked the General Law Committee in 2025 and 2026 for an equity-joint-venture exit after three years.
Records show Fine Fettle's chief operating officer supplied proposed statutory text.
Records show the Council's own bill, HB 5351, kept a seven-year bar subject to Council policy.
Records show the enacted rule allows exit after five years, with 90 days' notice, an optional non-binding Council review, and an $8,000 fee plus loan payoff.
Records show that mechanism first appears in House Amendment 'A' to HB 5350 (LCO 4259), offered by Representatives Lemar, Turco and Rojas, at lines 2758 to 2809.
It is absent from every earlier 2026 bill version the project holds.
LCO 4259 is a strike-everything amendment.
Records show the fiscal note does not quantify the exit mechanism.
Five years sits between the recorded positions: three years asked by industry and seven in the Council's bill.

According to the story card, operators' exit requests and the 2026 law were reported (Andrew Brown, CT Mirror, 8 April 2025; Katherine Revello, Inside Investigator, April-May 2026; Emilia Otte, CT Mirror, April-May 2026; a law-firm alert, 8 May 2026).
The project adds the provision-level trail: where the mechanism first appears, who offered that amendment, and how it compares with each recorded position.
Who drafted the mechanism is not established.
The sequence is documented, but influence is not established.
Five years is consistent with a negotiated compromise, and appearing in a strike-all amendment does not prove a provision was first added there.
Records show P.A. 25-101, a DCP agency bill (sHB 6855), removed the rule that equity-joint-venture retailers sharing a backer be at least 20 miles apart.
Records show the cultivator-backer piece took effect on 1 July 2025 and the rest on 1 January 2026.
According to the committee report, the bill was raised at DCP's request.
Records show the change was public: the OLR summary headlined it.
Records show a social-equity owner and Fine Fettle opposed it at the 14 February 2025 hearing as a safeguard against clustering.
No press coverage was located; the change appears in official legislative summaries.
The project identifies the repeal, its route through an agency bill and the hearing opposition.
Who inside or outside DCP asked for the repeal is not in the record.
The 20-mile clause for one licence type was itself only added in 2023, so the repeal may be agency clean-up.
Payroll records show Bryan Cafferelli moved from DCP staff attorney (2017-2019) to Legislative Management (2019-2023) and became DCP Commissioner in April 2023.
Payroll records show Shirley Skyers-Thomas moved from Legislative Management staff (2018 to June 2023) to DCP Deputy Commissioner in July 2023.
Payroll records show former Representative Brandon McGee left the House in January 2022 and became the Council's Executive Director in September 2024, after serving as Deputy Housing Commissioner.
Payroll records show Andrea Comer was paid as DCP Deputy Commissioner from September 2021 to January 2023 while chairing the Council.
Records show she later sat on the Council as a Treasurer designee, including at the 7 March 2023 vote.
Records show the statute provides for both DCP and Treasurer designees on the Council.
Payroll records show Council appointee Avery Gaddis was a permanent Legislative Management employee from 2015 to 2025.
Legislative-branch employment does not disqualify an appointee under CGS 21a-420d(b).
According to the ledger, these moves were reported (CT Mirror, 27 February 2023 and 7 August 2024; Hartford Business Journal, 2022).
The project adds only exact payroll dates and minute-level confirmation.
No ethics opinion, recusal issue or revolving-door violation has been identified.
These are ordinary career paths, and the statute expressly contemplates agency designees.
Records show the Council approved Caring Nature EJV1 and EJV2 as equity joint ventures on 7 March 2023.
Records show Verano's fiscal 2022 10-K lists both at 50% in its table of 'owned subsidiaries and entities over which the Company has control'.
Records show both appear on Verano's subsidiary lists for fiscal 2022 to 2025.
Records show Verano adds that its percentages 'may not match state regulatory records'.
Records show Caring Nature EJV2 signed in the guarantor pages of Verano's 11 March 2026 credit agreement.
Records show the signatory was James Leventis, Verano's Chief Strategy and Compliance Officer, as 'Authorized Signatory'.
Records show up to four other Connecticut ventures also appear as guarantors: Willow Brook Stratford, Willow Brook Enfield, and CTPharma Newington and Norwich.
The guarantor schedules are not public.

According to the story card, the Council's approval of Verano-backed retailers (Skyler Frazer, Hartford Business Journal, 8 March 2023) and Verano's March 2026 term loan were reported, without guarantor detail.
The project adds Verano's own control-table and subsidiary statements over four years and the ventures' guarantor signatures on parent debt.
Control under CGS 21a-420 is not established; accounting consolidation is a different legal test.

glossary.d: The Responsible and Equitable Regulation of Adult-Use Cannabis Act, the body of law created by June Sp. Sess. P.A. 21-1.
A bill that has passed both chambers and been signed or allowed to become law. The enacted act, not the published chapter page, is the authoritative text.
A committee’s replacement text for a raised bill. Where language first appears in a substitute, the committee record is the earliest source.
The number the Legislative Commissioners’ Office assigns to an amendment. A called amendment was voted on; an uncalled amendment was filed and never voted, and is evidence of what was asked for.
A numbered printing of a bill as reported out. Fiscal notes and bill analyses are written against a file copy, so the file number dates the analysis.
A company at least fifty per cent owned AND controlled by a person meeting the social equity criteria, sponsored by an existing licensed establishment. Two limbs, not one.
Defined by income and residency criteria. Connecticut publishes no list of which licensees are social equity licensees.
A person with a direct or indirect financial interest in a cannabis establishment who must register. The register carries no field saying which establishment a backer backs.
A converted medical dispensary facility selling to both patients and adult-use customers.
A disproportionately impacted area cultivator: a route to a cultivator licence outside the lottery, on payment of a substantial fee.
An agency document that is NOT a regulation adopted under chapter 54. The distinction decides what survives a challenge.
The committee’s report recommending a bill. Its testimony summary is committee staff’s account, not the witness’s words.
